title: Photo Composition: 10 Techniques and a Pre-Shot Checklist — cv.cm
description: Photo composition techniques for any phone or camera: leading lines, framing, symmetry, negative space, foreground and layers, plus a pre-shot checklist.
h1: How do you compose a good photo?
answer: Good composition means deciding what the subject is, then arranging the frame so the eye goes there first. Pick one subject, clean up the background, keep the horizon level, use lines, frames and foreground to lead to the subject, and leave out anything that does not help. Move your feet before you zoom: a step left or a lower angle often fixes more than any setting.

body: Most weak photos have no clear subject. Before you raise the camera, finish this sentence: this photo is about the old man feeding birds, or the red door, or the light on the water. If you cannot name it, the viewer will not find it either.

Once you know the subject, every other choice serves it. Where you stand, how close you go, what you leave in and what you leave out all depend on making that one thing easy to see. The techniques below are tools for that job. You do not need all of them in one photo. Two or three that fit the scene are enough.

head: Technique
What it does
How to do it
rows: Rule of thirds
Off-center placement that feels balanced
Turn on the 3x3 grid; put the subject or eyes on a line or crossing point
Leading lines
Guides the eye to the subject
Use roads, rails, fences, rivers, shadows; let them point at the subject, not out of the frame
Framing
Draws attention and adds depth
Shoot through a doorway, window, arch or branches so they surround the subject
Symmetry
Calm, strong, formal look
Center the line of symmetry exactly; check both sides match
Negative space
Makes a small subject stand out
Leave a large plain area such as sky, wall, water or sand around the subject
Foreground interest
Gives depth to wide scenes
Get low and include rocks, flowers or a path a short distance from the lens
Layers
Front, middle and back each add information
Look for something near, something in the middle, and a background; keep them from overlapping awkwardly
Fill the frame
Removes clutter and shows detail
Step closer until the subject fills most of the picture
Odd numbers
Groups of three or five look natural
Arrange or choose groups of three objects or people rather than two or four when you can
Patterns and breaks
Rhythm, then a point of interest
Fill the frame with a repeating pattern; include one element that breaks it

body: Leading lines are strongest when they start near the bottom corners and run toward the subject. A wide lens and a low camera position make lines in the foreground look longer and more dramatic. Lines that run out of the frame take the viewer with them, so turn until they point inward.
Framing works best when the frame is darker or plainer than the subject. A dark doorway around a bright street scene is clear. A busy frame around a busy scene is not.

sections.h: Keep the horizon level and the verticals straight
body: A tilted horizon is the fastest way to make a good photo look careless. Turn on the grid and the level on your phone or camera. On a phone the level is usually a line that changes color when it is straight.

Tall buildings lean backward when you tilt the camera up. Step back and keep the phone upright, or use a wider lens and crop later. For a deliberate tilt, make it strong, around 15 to 30 degrees, so it looks chosen and not accidental.
Water must always be flat. If a lake or sea runs downhill in your photo, straighten it in editing, even if you crop a little.

sections.h: Check the background and the edges
body: Our eyes ignore clutter when we stand in a scene. The camera records all of it. Before you press the shutter, look away from the subject and scan the rest of the frame.

ul: Poles, trees or lamp posts that seem to grow out of a person's head. Move one step sideways.
Bright spots near the edges, such as a white car, a window or a sign. Bright areas pull the eye away from the subject.
Cut-off body parts at the joints: wrists, ankles, knees and elbows. Crop between joints instead, for example at mid-thigh.
A horizon or wall line running through a person's neck. Raise or lower the camera so the line passes behind the shoulders or above the head.
Strangers looking at the camera in the background. Wait, change the angle, or use a wider aperture to blur them. Respect people who do not want to be photographed.

body: If the background cannot be fixed, simplify it. Go closer, shoot from a low angle against the sky, use portrait mode or a wide aperture to blur it, or turn so a plain wall is behind the subject.

sections.h: Angle and distance: move before you zoom
body: Most people shoot everything from standing eye height. Changing height is often the biggest single improvement.

ul: Low angle: crouch to make a child, a pet or a building look larger and to put the sky behind the subject.
Eye level: the natural choice for portraits of adults, children and animals. Go down to their eye height.
High angle or overhead: shows patterns, food on a table, or how things are arranged.
Closer: if the photo feels empty, take two steps forward before you zoom. Distance changes the relationship between subject and background, zoom only crops.
Further back with a longer lens: on a phone, use the 2x or 3x camera for portraits to make the background look closer and the face more natural.

body: Take the first shot, then take three more from different positions: closer, lower, and from the side. Choose later. Burst mode helps with moving subjects.

sections.h: Composition checklist before you press the shutter

ol: Can I name the subject in a few words?
Is the subject the brightest, sharpest or most colorful thing in the frame?
Is focus on the subject? On a phone, tap it on the screen.
Is the horizon level and are verticals upright?
Is anything growing out of a head, or cut at a joint?
Are there bright distractions at the edges?
Do the lines in the scene point to the subject?
Is there space in the direction the subject looks or moves?
Would it be better closer, lower, or from the side?
Is the orientation right: vertical for one standing person, horizontal for wide places?

body.note: This takes about five seconds once it becomes a habit. Most professionals do it without thinking, but they still do it.

head: What you see in the photo
Cause
Fix
rows: Subject is tiny in a busy scene
Shot from too far away
Walk closer or use the 2x or 3x lens; fill the frame
Photo feels flat, no depth
Everything is at the same distance
Add foreground, shoot through something, or include layers
Eye wanders and does not settle
Two or more subjects compete
Choose one; leave the other out or make it smaller
Person looks squeezed
No space in the direction they face
Place them on the opposite third line
Sea or horizon slopes
Phone held at a slight angle
Turn on the level; straighten when editing
Every photo looks the same
Always shooting from standing height
Try one low and one high angle for each scene

body: After shooting, cropping can still improve composition. Remove an empty edge, straighten the horizon, or move the subject to a third. cv.cm's crop and rotate tools do this in the browser without uploading the photo.

faq.q: What are the basic elements of composition in photography?
faq.a: The usual elements are subject, line, shape, pattern, texture, color, space and balance. In practice, most good compositions combine a clear subject, a clean background, and one or two devices such as leading lines or framing.

faq.q: Is composition more important than camera quality?
faq.a: For most viewers, yes. A well-composed photo from a phone usually looks better than a badly composed photo from an expensive camera. Better equipment helps most in low light and with fast action.

faq.q: How can I practice photo composition?
faq.a: Pick one technique a day, such as leading lines, and shoot only that. Then look at your photos and ask what the subject is and whether the eye goes there first. Studying photos you like and copying their structure also helps.

faq.q: Should I compose in camera or crop later?
faq.a: Compose in camera as well as you can, but leave a little extra space around the edges. Cropping later is useful for straightening and fine-tuning, but it cannot add what you did not capture.

faq.q: What is negative space in photography?
faq.a: Negative space is the empty area around the subject, such as plain sky, water or a wall. Used on purpose, it makes the subject stand out and gives the photo a calm, simple look.
